definitions.definition: Anything that can be offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use or consumption, including physical objects, services, places, organisations and ideas.
Having built something that solves a real problem for a specific group of people who actively use it, recommend it and will pay for it.
Different layers of value that a product offers a customer, ranging from core benefit to potential product.
The service or benefit the customer is really buying.
Form into which the marketer turns the core benefit, such as a hotel room with a bed, bathroom and towels.
Set of attributes and conditions that buyers normally expect when they purchase the product.
Level of the offering that exceeds customer expectations, for example a complimentary breakfast at a hotel.
Everything an offering can become in the future, focusing on innovation, growth and long-term competitiveness rather than today's features.
Number of different product lines that a company carries.
Total number of items in the mix of a company.
Number of variants offered of each product in the line.
Removing weak or non-performing items from a line so the company can focus on profitable, high-demand ones.
Situation in which a new offering takes sales away from a company's existing offering instead of attracting new customers.
Goods bought and consumed by the end customer.
Class of goods that are used for the manufacturing of other goods.
Class of products such as tools, machinery, buildings, vehicles and computers.
Any product perceived by the customer as new, such as a repositioned product, a lower-priced existing product or an added product item.
Developed form of a product idea that consumers actually buy, since consumers do not buy mere ideas.
Creative technique that improves existing products or ideas by asking guided questions to modify something.
Creative technique for generating many ideas in a short time through free thinking without criticism or judgment.
Creative problem-solving technique that uses analogies, mentally taking things apart and putting them together to give new insight.
Analytical approach to recognise new forms of a system or product by identifying areas of improvement.
Technique that joins totally different ideas to come up with a fresh idea, often yielding useful combinations.
Cross-functional approach that involves many business function areas throughout the entire product innovation cycle.
Examination of financial information to reach business decisions.
Systematic evaluation of all costs associated with launching a new product to support pricing, budgeting and profitability decisions.
Process of planning activities that make customers aware of a product and encourage them to buy it.
Promotion of products or services using digital technologies such as the internet, websites, social media, search engines, email and mobile apps.
Performance-based method in which an individual or business earns a commission for promoting and selling another company's products.
Form of digital promotion that uses popular online creators to advertise products or services to their established audience.
Business process of selling goods or services directly to individual consumers for their personal, non-business use.
Process allowing customers to search, select and purchase products, services and information remotely over the Internet.
Process of evaluating a product's performance after launch, to decide whether it achieved its marketing and business objectives.
An act or use for which a consumer, company or government is willing to pay, an intangible performance through which the provider adds value.
Characteristic of services that they are not manufactured, transported or stocked.
Characteristic of services that they are produced and consumed simultaneously, so the consumer must be present for delivery.
Characteristic of services that each one is unique, can never be exactly repeated and is typically modified for each consumer.
Characteristic of services by which a rendered service irreversibly vanishes and unused capacity is lost.
Two-by-three matrix that classifies services by the number of delivery sites and the method of delivery.
Set of marketing tools that a firm uses to pursue its marketing objectives in the target market.
Extra service-marketing element covering the human actors who participate in service delivery.
Extra service-marketing element covering the set of activities that results in delivery of the benefits of an offering.
Extra service-marketing element covering the tangible setting and cues that facilitate performance and communication of the service.
The environment in which a service is assembled and in which the seller and customer interact.
Controllable factors of a physical service setting, such as temperature, air, sound, light, music and scent.
Activity of planning and arranging the people, infrastructure, communication and material components of a service.

definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Moment at which the user interacts with a service.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Service design principle that all stakeholders should be included in the design process, since a service exists only with user participation.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Network of people, organisations and activities necessary to transfer ownership of goods from producer to consumer.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Party authorised to act for a principal to facilitate exchange, typically without taking title to the goods.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Arrangement in which the producer or service provider handles delivery itself, without intermediaries.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Approach of stocking a product in as many outlets as possible, which suits mass-produced goods.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Approach in which the producer uses a limited number of intermediaries, often specialist dealers.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Approach in which the producer works with a single intermediary, giving the manufacturer more control and typical of luxury goods.
definitions.unitTitle: Service Process Design and Service Distribution

definitions.definition: Comparison of the perceived expectations of a service with its perceived performance.
Difference between customer expectations and perceptions, the only gap that can be measured directly.
Model identifying five gaps between expected and experienced service that cause unsuccessful service delivery.
Scale that measures customer perception of service quality by comparing what customers expect with what they receive.
Service quality dimension of delivering the promised service dependably and on time.
Service quality dimension covering staff behaviour that builds customer confidence.
Service quality dimension covering the appearance of physical facilities, equipment and materials.
Service quality dimension of giving customers individual attention and convenient access.
Service quality dimension of willingness to help customers and provide prompt service.
Costs that would disappear if systems, processes and products were perfect.
